<b>Hacia 1000</b>Ibn al-Haytham (Alhacén: Around 1000Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) studies refraction and reflection in his "Book of Optics"; in the 13th century Kamal al-Din al-Farisi explains the rainbow with a water-filled sphere as a model of a drop.
<b>1304</b>Teodorico de Freiberg hace lo: 1304Theodoric of Freiberg does the same with a glass sphere filled with water and traces the path of the light: two refractions and one reflection inside the drop.
<b>1637</b>René Descartes, en «Los meteo: 1637René Descartes, in "Les Météores", uses the law of sines to calculate the 42° angle and sees that the rays pile up at the minimum deviation. He does not yet explain the colours.
<b>1666</b>Isaac Newton hace pasar la lu: 1666Isaac Newton passes sunlight through a prism and shows that each colour is refracted differently; with this he explains the order of the colours of the bow (Opticks, 1704).
<b>1803</b>Thomas Young explica los arco: 1803Thomas Young explains supernumerary arcs, the faint coloured fringes inside the main bow, with the interference of light; in 1908 Gustav Mie accurately calculates the scattering of light by droplets.

Un rayo del Sol llega a una gota de agua: A ray from the Sun reaches a drop of water. At the surface it passes from air ($n = 1$) to water ($n = ${f3(N)}$), where light goes more slowly, and bends towards the normal: this is Snell's law, $"sin" i = n "sin" r$.\n\nFor a ray arriving with $i = ${f1(i0)}°$ we get $"sin" r = "sin" ${f1(i0)}° / ${f3(N)}$, that is $r = ${f1(r0)}°$. Each ray that enters the drop at a different place does so with a different $i$, from 0° (at the centre) to 90° (grazing).

Al llegar al fondo de la gota, parte de: On reaching the back of the drop, part of the light is reflected (the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, $r$) and returns to the front face, where it leaves, refracting again, this time from water to air.\n\nIn total the ray turns $(i − r) + (180° − 2r) + (i − r)$, that is, $D = 180° + 2i − 4r$. With $i = ${f1(i0)}°$ and $r = ${f1(r0)}°$ this gives $D = ${f1(D0)}°$: the light leaves almost in the opposite direction to the one it had, at $180° − D = ${f1(a0)}°$ from the direction back to the Sun.

Los rayos del Sol que llegan a una gota: The rays of the Sun reaching a drop do not all enter with the same $i$. Each one leaves at its own angle, but the angle $180° − D$ does not grow endlessly: it rises to a maximum of ${f1(a0)}° (with $i = ${f1(i0)}°$) and falls again.\n\nNear a maximum the curve is flat, so many different rays leave in almost the same direction and add up: there is intense light there. Beyond ${f0(a0)}° none comes out. Descartes discovered it in 1637 by tracing rays by hand through a sphere of water.
